title: Power-seeking without the symmetry condition: in random deterministic MDPs the higher-POWER action is usually, but not always, the more probably optimal one
abstract: Turner et al. (arXiv:1912.01683) prove that when one action's set of reachable visit-distribution functions contains a permuted copy of another's (Proposition 6.9), the first action leads to at least as much expected POWER and, under a reachability condition, is at least as likely to be optimal, for most reward distributions. For an IID state-reward distribution the 'most' ordering reduces to a plain inequality, so the result can be checked numerically. The copy condition almost never holds exactly in an arbitrary environment; we ask how often its conclusion survives without it. Method (pre-registered before any run): deterministic MDPs, state rewards IID uniform on [0,1], exact optimal values by policy iteration (checked against 40,000 sweeps of value iteration: largest difference $1.1\times10^{-10}$), 4000 reward samples per instance and discount rate $\gamma \in \{0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999\}$. Part A: 200 constructed MDPs that satisfy both conditions of Proposition 6.9 (checked programmatically). No instance-$\gamma$ pair met the falsifier (optimality probability of the copy-containing action below 1/2 at one-sided $p<10^{-4}$, or a POWER deficit beyond 4 standard errors); the lowest optimality probability, 0.478 at $\gamma=0.1$, is $z=-2.8$ among 1000 pairs, consistent with noise. Part B: 1000 random MDPs with 20 states, out-degree uniform on {1,2,3}, the start state having two distinct successors. Among instances where one action is decidedly more probably optimal ($z>3$) and the successors' POWER differs by more than 3 standard errors, the higher-POWER action is the more probably optimal one in 95.3% (836/877, Wilson 95% interval 93.7 to 96.5%) at $\gamma=0.99$ and 96.4% (94.9 to 97.4%) at $\gamma=0.9$. Reversals are real: 41 of 877 decided instances at $\gamma=0.99$ (4.7%, 3.5 to 6.3%), and all 115 reversal pairs across discount rates were confirmed on $10^5$ fresh reward samples (smallest $|z|$ 7.4 for optimality probability, smallest POWER difference 8.4 standard errors). In a reversal the mean and median of the successors' value difference have opposite signs: POWER is an expectation, optimality probability a sign probability, and without the symmetry condition nothing forces them to agree. A crude option count (states reachable from each successor) agrees with optimality in only 73.8% (66.7 to 79.9%) of the 168 decided instances at $\gamma=0.99$ where the counts differ, below POWER's agreement, and is uninformative in the other 733 of 901, where the counts are equal. The share of decided instances rises with $\gamma$, from 14.6% at 0.1 to 90.1% at 0.99. Limitations: one random-graph model at one size, one reward distribution, deterministic transitions and exact optimal (not learned) policies; agreement rates are conditional on the decided and untied thresholds; Part A is a consistency check of a proved result, able to detect a gap but not to add support to the theorem. This is a numerical study, not a new theorem, and says nothing directly about trained agents.

claims.text: In 200 constructed deterministic MDPs satisfying both conditions of Turner et al.'s Proposition 6.9, with IID uniform state rewards and $\gamma$ in {0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999}, no instance shows the copy-containing action optimal with probability below 1/2 at one-sided $p<10^{-4}$, nor its successor's POWER lower by more than 4 standard errors.

In random deterministic MDPs (20 states, out-degree uniform on {1,2,3}, IID uniform state rewards) at $\gamma=0.99$, among start states where one of two actions is decidedly more probably optimal and the successors' POWER differs, the higher-POWER action is the more probably optimal one in 95.3% of instances (95% CI 93.7 to 96.5%).

In the same random deterministic MDPs, the higher-POWER action is decidedly less probably optimal in 4.7% (95% CI 3.5 to 6.3%) of decided, POWER-untied instances at $\gamma=0.99$, and every such reversal found at 4000 reward samples is confirmed at $10^5$ samples.

In the same random deterministic MDPs at $\gamma=0.99$, the action whose successor reaches more states is the more probably optimal one in 73.8% (95% CI 66.7 to 79.9%) of decided instances where reach counts differ, a lower agreement rate than POWER's.

builds_on.note: Reproduced the IID consequence of Proposition 6.9 (v10) numerically: 200 constructed MDPs satisfying both conditions, 5 discount rates, no violation of either ordering. Then used Definition 5.2 (POWER) unchanged to measure how often its conclusion holds where the copy condition fails.
